name: Kazachok
short_status: Built, tested, mated to the rover and never launched. ESA suspended the ExoMars cooperation with Roscosmos on 17 March 2022 and terminated it in July; Roscosmos said the platform was home in Russia on 30 October 2024.
tagline: Roscosmos, with ESA · Multinational · Lander · 2015 · Multipolar Mars Cancelled
stats: platform mass, including a 45 kg science payload
instruments built, tested and integrated: 11 Russian and two European
science instruments on the European lander that replaced it

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: The surface platform of the ExoMars 2022 mission, the responsibility of Roscosmos and the Space Research Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, built by NPO Lavochkin. Once the rover had driven off, Kazachok would have remained where it landed and worked as a stationary automatic station, powered by solar panels and rechargeable batteries. ESA gives its nominal mission lifetime as one Earth year; the eoPortal mission entry gives about two Earth years, a figure that traces back to a 2018 conference abstract by the Russian science team.

facts.label: The name
facts.value: Казачок means little Cossack and is also an East Slavic folk dance. The name was announced by Roscosmos in March 2019 as the platform arrived in Europe. On 23 May 2019, speaking at Moscow State University, Roscosmos director general Dmitry Rogozin said what the alternative had been, in remarks RIA Novosti reported: "Я, правда, хотел назвать его «Новичком», но решил, что коллеги не поймут" ("I did actually want to call it Novichok, but decided my colleagues would not get it"). Novichok is the name of a class of nerve agent, and in 2019 the word carried an obvious diplomatic charge.

facts.label: Mass and payload
facts.value: ESA gives the surface platform a mass of 827.9 kg including a scientific payload of 45 kg. Korablev, Rodionov and Zelenyi's 2024 paper in Solar System Research gives the same 45 kg for the instrument complex, and counts it as 11 Russian and two European instruments.

facts.label: The instruments
facts.value: Two European-led: LaRa, a Belgian radio science experiment measuring the rotation and orientation of Mars from Doppler shifts, and HABIT, a Swedish package on water vapour, ground and air temperature and ultraviolet radiation. Eleven Russian-led: METEO M (meteorology), MAIGRET (magnetometer), TSPP (four cameras), BIP (instrument interface and memory), FAST (infrared Fourier spectrometer), ADRON-EM (active neutron spectrometer and dosimeter), M-DLS (diode laser spectrometer), PAT-M (radio thermometer reading soil to 1 m), Dust Suite, SEM (seismometer) and MGAP (gas chromatograph mass spectrometer). Four European sensor packages sat inside METEO M and MAIGRET, from Finland, Spain and the Czech Republic.

facts.label: What it was for
facts.value: Korablev, Rodionov and Zelenyi list the objectives as long-term climate monitoring, atmospheric composition, the mechanisms of dust lifting and the electrical phenomena that go with them, interactions between atmosphere and surface, the abundance of water in the subsurface layer, radiation monitoring, and the internal structure of Mars. ESA adds that the radiation measurements were to be compared with the dosimeter on FREND aboard the Trace Gas Orbiter.

facts.label: How it would have landed
facts.value: A European carrier module would have released the Russian descent module before entry. Aerodynamic braking and then parachutes would shed most of the speed, and the final braking and touchdown would have been done by the platform's own throttleable rocket engines, with the rover driving off down a ramp afterwards. ESA states that the parachute system was fully qualified, with a supersonic parachute from a United States manufacturer and a European subsonic one.

facts.label: Built in Russia, tested in Italy
facts.value: Roscosmos recorded that on 19 March 2019 the flight article of the Kazachok landing platform, manufactured and assembled at NPO Lavochkin, was shipped to Thales Alenia Space in Italy for testing, packed to planetary protection requirements and accompanied by ground support equipment. Components of the descent module, its onboard equipment, batteries, aerodynamic shield and back cover, followed in stages through 2019. Lavochkin was the head coordinator on the Russian side and the developer and manufacturer of the descent module with its landing platform.

facts.label: The schedule it lost
facts.value: Launch on a Proton-M with a Briz-M upper stage from Baikonur in a window running 20 September to 1 October 2022, with arrival at Oxia Planum on 10 June 2023 after about 264 days of cruise; RBC, reporting the same plan, wrote only that the landing was expected by June 2023. ESA states that the spacecraft was ready to move to the launch campaign at Baikonur in April 2022 and was halted. The 2022 window was the third: the mission had slipped from 2018 to 2020, then on 12 March 2020 from 2020 to 2022 because of outstanding testing and the COVID-19 pandemic.

facts.label: The decision, as written
facts.value: ESA press release N° 9-2022, dated 17 March 2022: "ESA's ruling Council, meeting in Paris on 16-17 March, assessed the situation arising from the war in Ukraine regarding ExoMars, and unanimously: acknowledged the present impossibility of carrying out the ongoing cooperation with Roscosmos on the ExoMars rover mission with a launch in 2022, and mandated the ESA Director General to take appropriate steps to suspend the cooperation activities accordingly; authorised the ESA Director General to carry out a fast-track industrial study to better define the available options for a way forward to implement the ExoMars rover mission."

facts.label: Suspension is not termination
facts.value: March 2022 suspended the cooperation. Termination came four months later. Roscosmos stated that on 12 July 2022 the ESA Director General notified it, in accordance with a decision of the ESA Council of member states, that ESA had terminated the bilateral cooperation on the ExoMars 2022 mission because of the complex geopolitical situation, and that both sides were working on options for returning Russian equipment held in the European Union and European equipment held in Russia. ESA's own public FAQ dates the Council decision only to July 2022 without a day.

facts.label: Russia said it would build another
facts.value: On 23 March 2022 Roscosmos said its Mars programme would now need a new landing platform, and quoted director general Dmitry Rogozin: "Повторить посадочный модуль «Казачок», который мы делали под миссию ExoMars, не представляет труда. Все чертежи есть, это наша работа" ("Repeating the Kazachok landing module that we made for the ExoMars mission is no trouble. All the drawings exist, this is our work"). No such module has been announced since, and no Russian Mars mission appears in the national space project running to 2036.

facts.label: Getting it home took two and a half years
facts.value: On 23 March 2022 Roscosmos said it could not bring the descent module back from Europe at all, because European Union airspace was closed to Russian aircraft, and that its Mars programme would therefore need a new landing platform. On 26 March 2023 Roscosmos said it had agreed a plan of mutual return with ESA and that its staff were already working at Thales Alenia Space in Turin. On 30 October 2024 Tatyana Tishchenko, director of the Roscosmos international cooperation department, told the outlet Pro Kosmos that the platform and all other Russian hardware were back in Russia, except for individual items of foreign-made ground test equipment for which the European Union had not granted re-export permission.

facts.label: The Russian instruments on the rover
facts.value: Two Russian instruments were riding on Rosalind Franklin itself: ISEM, an infrared spectrometer, and ADRON-RM, a neutron spectrometer for subsurface water ice. Both were dismounted and returned with the rest of the Russian hardware. The infrared spectrometer has been replaced by a British-built instrument, ENFYS, led by Aberystwyth University, a test model of which shipped to Turin in October 2025; ESA states that the neutron spectrometer will not be replaced at all. Roscosmos's own comment on the removal, in March 2023: "мы можем только пожелать нашим коллегам из ЕКА успешно осуществить запуск марсохода в октябре 2028 года без нашего участия" ("we can only wish our colleagues at ESA a successful launch of the rover in October 2028 without our participation").

facts.label: What replaced it
facts.value: A new European entry, descent and landing module, funded by ESA member states at the November 2022 ministerial council. ESA plans to reuse the qualified onboard computer, the radar Doppler altimeter and the parachute system that had been built as European equipment for the Russian descent module. Thales Alenia Space is the industrial lead, Airbus provides the landing platform, and Sener in Spain designed and built the legs. On 6 August 2026 ESA published footage of those legs deploying in pairs in under a second on a full-scale model in Turin, and repeated a landing in 2030.

facts.label: The science did not survive
facts.value: ESA states that to make a 2028 launch the lander design is simplified and the new landing platform will be built only to deliver the rover and let it drive off. It will carry engineering sensors and some cameras to validate European landing technology, but no dedicated solar arrays and no science complement, and will stop working a few sols after touchdown once the rover has its arrays open and a link to Earth. Kazachok's thirteen instruments have no successor on the mission.

timeline: ESA calls on the European scientific community for surface platform instruments in March, receives nine proposals, and in November approves six European elements: two European-led instruments, LaRa and HABIT, and four sensor packages inside two Russian-led instruments.

The flight article of the landing platform, built and assembled at NPO Lavochkin, is flown to Thales Alenia Space in Italy for testing, packed to planetary protection requirements. Roscosmos announces its name at the same time: Kazachok.
Rogozin tells an audience at Moscow State University that he had wanted to call the module Novichok and decided his colleagues would not get it.

ESA and Roscosmos announce the launch slips from July 2020 to the August to October 2022 window, citing the need for more testing of hardware and final software and the travel restrictions of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The descent module with Kazachok is at Thales Alenia Space in Turin with the Rosalind Franklin rover mounted on it. The launch window is 20 September to 1 October 2022 and the landing at Oxia Planum is expected by June 2023.

ESA's Council, meeting in Paris, unanimously acknowledges the present impossibility of carrying out the cooperation with Roscosmos on the ExoMars rover mission with a launch in 2022, and mandates the Director General to suspend it. The spacecraft was due to move to the Baikonur launch campaign in April.

Roscosmos says it cannot return the descent module with Kazachok from Europe because European Union airspace is closed to Russian aircraft, and that a Russian Mars programme will therefore need a new landing platform. Rogozin: reproducing Kazachok is no trouble, all the drawings exist, this is our work.

With the launch campaign cancelled, the ExoMars elements are prepared for storage at a Thales Alenia Space site in Italy to await further instruction. The rover and the platform, mated and tested, go into a clean room instead of a Proton fairing.

ESA's Director General notifies Roscosmos, under a decision of the ESA Council of member states, that the bilateral cooperation on ExoMars 2022 is terminated. Both sides begin work on returning each other's hardware.
At ESA's ministerial council, member states commit to fund a new mission, with a new European lander to carry Rosalind Franklin to the surface. Kazachok has no role in it.

Roscosmos announces a plan of mutual return agreed with ESA, with its staff already at work in Turin, and confirms that the Russian instruments on the rover, ADRON-RM and ISEM, will be dismounted. It wishes ESA a successful launch in October 2028 without Russian participation.

Tatyana Tishchenko of Roscosmos says the Kazachok platform and all other Russian hardware are back on Russian territory, apart from foreign-made ground test equipment refused re-export permission by the European Union. She adds that Roscosmos hopes for joint Mars and Venus expeditions with China and India.

images.caption: The Kazachok landing platform in the clean room at Thales Alenia Space in Turin in November 2020, sitting on a supporting trolley with its ramps and solar panels folded, while the dark rear jacket of the descent module hangs from a red lifting frame directly above it and engineers work at floor level. ESA's caption records that the front shield would later be fitted to the same trolley, and that the platform and the Rosalind Franklin rover would then undergo joint testing at Cannes.
images.credit: Thales Alenia Space (credit line given on the ESA image page)

images.caption: The Rosalind Franklin rover in its stowed configuration sitting on top of the Kazachok surface platform in a clean room at Thales Alenia Space in Cannes, two of the platform's ramps deployed down to the floor on either side and one of its solar panels partially deployed at the front left, the platform itself standing on a wheeled support trolley rather than on its own landing legs. ESA's caption records that the two were mated to form the landing module and that the tests included electrical, power and data transfer checks between them.
images.credit: Thales Alenia Space (credit line given on the ESA image page)

images.caption: The Russian landing platform suspended from a hoist as it is unpacked in Turin in March 2019, its white upper panels and the dark frame of its ramps visible, with a technician in a clean-room suit steadying it. ESA's caption records that the platform left Russia in March 2019 packed to planetary protection requirements, flew to Turin on an Antonov with its ground support equipment, and that Roscosmos announced its new name, Kazachok, at this point.
images.credit: Thales Alenia Space (credit line given on the ESA image page)

images.caption: A Lavochkin computer drawing of the landing platform from above and from below, labelled in Russian for марсоход (the rover), трапы (the ramps), панели СБ (the solar panels), служебная и научная аппаратура (the service and science equipment), баки с топливом (the propellant tanks) and посадочные опоры (the landing legs).

A Lavochkin diagram of the entry, descent and landing sequence drawn over a Martian horizon and keyed in Russian with times, altitudes and speeds: entry at t equals 0 at 120 km and 6.1 km/s, peak heating, first stage of the parachute system, main parachute, front shield separation, separation of the rear cover with the parachute, end of braking, engine cut-off and touchdown at about 1.2 to 1.45 m/s, then the landing platform deploying its solar panels and ramps.
